title: THE KING WHO TRUSTED GOD FOR VICTORY… BUT COULDN’T TRUST HIM WITH HIS PAIN
paragraphs: THE KING WHO TRUSTED GOD FOR VICTORY… BUT COULDN’T TRUST HIM WITH HIS PAIN

Why did King Asa develop a severe disease in his feet? The disturbing truth behind 2 Chronicles 16:12–13—and the warning every Christian needs to hear before a heart that once trusted God learns to live without seeking Him.
He had watched God deliver an entire nation.
He had seen an impossible battle turn into a miraculous victory.
He had once stood before the Lord and confessed that human strength was nothing compared to the power of the Almighty.
But years later, when disease began consuming his feet, something was terribly wrong.
The man who once ran to God in desperation would not seek Him in his suffering.
And perhaps the most frightening part of King Asa's story is not that his feet became diseased.
It is that his heart had already begun walking away from the very God who had carried him.
Read that again.
Because this is not merely a story about an ancient king who became sick.

It is about what can happen when a believer experiences God's faithfulness, enjoys His blessings, survives impossible battles… and slowly begins trusting something else more than the One who delivered them.
And before we finish, there is a question buried inside this account that every one of us must answer.
What happens when the person who once depended on God begins treating God as a last resort?
The Bible records these chilling words:

"And Asa in the thirty and ninth year of his reign was diseased in his feet, until his disease was exceeding great: yet in his disease he sought not to the LORD, but to the physicians. And Asa slept with his fathers, and died in the one and fortieth year of his reign." — 2 Chronicles 16:12–13 (KJV)
At first glance, it sounds like a warning against doctors.
But that is not what Scripture teaches.
And if we misunderstand this passage, we risk missing the deeper tragedy entirely.
To understand why this faithful king ended his life under such a troubling shadow, we must return to the days when Asa was still a man who knew where his help came from.
Long before his feet became diseased, Asa was one of Judah's most remarkable reforming kings.
He removed foreign altars, destroyed places of idolatrous worship, and called the people to seek the Lord.
He was not perfect, but his early reign was marked by an extraordinary determination to turn Judah back toward the God of their fathers.
Then came a crisis.
A massive army marched against Judah.
According to 2 Chronicles 14:9, Zerah the Ethiopian advanced with an army described as a thousand thousand men and three hundred chariots.
The biblical account presents Judah facing an overwhelming military threat.
Asa could have surrendered to fear.
He could have placed his confidence in weapons, military calculations, or the strength of his soldiers.
Instead, he prayed.
And the words of his prayer reveal the heart of the man he once was.

"LORD, it is nothing with thee to help, whether with many, or with them that have no power: help us, O LORD our God; for we rest on thee, and in thy name we go against this multitude." — 2 Chronicles 14:11 (KJV)
"For we rest on thee."
What a confession.
Not "We have enough soldiers."
Not "Our strategy is unbeatable."
Not "We have everything under control."
We rest on You.
The Hebrew text includes the words:
כִּי־עָלֶיךָ נִשְׁעַנּוּ
Ki 'alekha nish'annu.
Meaning, in context, "For we rely on You."
The verb comes from the Hebrew root שׁען (sha'an), expressing the idea of leaning upon or depending on someone for support.
Picture that.
A king standing before an overwhelming enemy, confessing that his nation was leaning upon God.
Not merely believing God existed.
Not merely respecting God's commandments.
Actually depending on Him.
And Scripture tells us that the Lord struck the enemy before Asa and Judah (2 Chronicles 14:12).
The victory was God's.
The deliverance was God's.
The glory belonged to God.
But here is where this story becomes painfully personal.
Sometimes the greatest danger to our faith does not come before the miracle.
Sometimes it comes after we have survived it.
When we are desperate, we pray.
When the diagnosis frightens us, we cry out.
When our finances collapse, we seek the Lord.
When our family is falling apart, we open our Bibles with trembling hands.
But when life becomes manageable again…
When the income stabilizes…
When the relationship improves…
When the emergency passes…
When our reputation is restored…
We can gradually begin living as though the God who rescued us is no longer necessary for the ordinary decisions of life.
We still attend church.
We still know the worship songs.
We still say, "God is good."
But somewhere beneath the religious language, our dependence has shifted.
And sometimes we do not recognize that shift until another crisis exposes it.
That is what makes Asa's later years so heartbreaking.
In the thirty-sixth year of his reign, according to 2 Chronicles 16:1, King Baasha of Israel came against Judah and fortified Ramah, threatening Asa's kingdom.
Once again, Asa faced a serious political and military crisis.
But this time, his response was different.

Instead of the prayer recorded in chapter 14, we read that Asa took silver and gold from the treasures of the house of the Lord and the king's house and sent them to Ben-hadad, king of Syria, seeking an alliance against Israel.
The plan worked in an immediate political sense.
Ben-hadad attacked Israelite cities.
Baasha stopped building Ramah.
Asa removed the building materials and used them to fortify other cities.
From a purely human perspective, Asa's strategy looked successful.
The threat had been neutralized.
The kingdom had gained relief.
The king could have congratulated himself.
But heaven saw something that political success could not reveal.
God sent Hanani the seer to confront him.
And Hanani's message exposed the problem.
"Because thou hast relied on the king of Syria, and not relied on the LORD thy God…" — 2 Chronicles 16:7 (KJV)
There it is.
The same issue that had once defined Asa's faith now exposed his decline.
Reliance.
The king who once leaned upon God had begun leaning upon another source of security instead.
And God reminded him of the earlier deliverance.
Had the Lord not rescued him when the Ethiopian and Libyan forces came against him?
Had Asa forgotten what God had already done?
Then came one of the most beautiful and searching declarations in the Old Testament.
"For the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to shew himself strong in the behalf of them whose heart is perfect toward him." — 2 Chronicles 16:9 (KJV)
In Hebrew, the description of the heart includes:
לְבָבָם שָׁלֵם אֵלָיו
Levavam shalem elav.
Their heart is whole, complete, or fully devoted toward Him.
The Hebrew word שָׁלֵם (shalem) carries the sense of wholeness or completeness.
This does not mean that God only helps people who have never sinned.
If that were true, none of us could stand before Him.
The emphasis is on a heart whose loyalty is undivided toward God.
A heart that truly belongs to Him.
A heart that does not merely acknowledge Him publicly while secretly placing its ultimate confidence somewhere else.
And suddenly Asa's story becomes a mirror.
Because it is possible to have a Christian reputation while developing a divided heart.
Possible to defend biblical truth in public while refusing God's correction in private.
Possible to remember the miracles of yesterday while no longer seeking the Lord today.
Possible to appear spiritually strong while becoming inwardly resistant to the very voice of God.
And here is the terrible turning point.
When Hanani confronted Asa, the king did not respond like David when Nathan exposed his sin.
He did not confess.
He did not humble himself.
He did not ask God for mercy.
Instead, Scripture says Asa became angry with the seer and put him in prison.
He also oppressed some of the people at that time (2 Chronicles 16:10).
The man who had once led his nation toward God was now punishing the messenger who called him back to God.
How does a person reach that point?
Not necessarily overnight.
Sometimes it happens through a thousand small refusals to repent.
A warning ignored.
A conviction suppressed.
An apology never offered.
A secret sin defended.
A Scripture passage avoided because it touches something we do not want to surrender.
Until eventually, correction begins to feel like an attack.
And the voice that could have helped us return to God becomes the voice we most want to silence.
Have you ever experienced that?
Someone lovingly confronts something in your life, and your first response is not repentance but defensiveness.
A sermon touches your pride, and instead of asking God to search your heart, you begin criticizing the preacher.
A friend points out a destructive pattern, and instead of listening, you withdraw.
You tell yourself they do not understand.
You convince yourself they are judging you.
But deep inside, there is a quieter possibility you do not want to face.
What if God is using that uncomfortable truth to call you back?
What if the wound you are trying to protect is the very place where repentance needs to begin?
And then, three years after the confrontation recorded in chapter 16, the Bible tells us something devastating.
Asa became diseased in his feet.
His condition grew exceedingly severe.
And in his illness, he did not seek the Lord.
He sought physicians.
The Hebrew of 2 Chronicles 16:12 reads, in part:
וַיֶּחֱלֶא אָסָא ... בְּרַגְלָיו
Vayyechele Asa ... beraglav.
"Asa became ill ... in his feet."
The verse describes the disease as:
עַד־לְמַעְלָה חָלְיוֹ
Ad-lema'lah cholyō.
An expression describing the severity of his illness, rendered in the KJV as "his disease was exceeding great."
But we must be careful here.
The Bible does not identify the exact medical condition.
It does not say Asa had gout, gangrene, diabetes, or any particular modern diagnosis.
Those suggestions sometimes appear in discussions of the passage, but they remain speculation.
We also cannot confidently claim that God directly inflicted this disease as a specific punishment.
The text does not explicitly say that.
What the inspired writer does emphasize is Asa's spiritual response to his suffering.
And that response is deeply troubling.
"Yet in his disease he sought not to the LORD, but to the physicians."
Notice what the passage does not say.
It does not say seeking medical care is sinful.
It does not command believers to reject physicians.
It does not teach that prayer and medical treatment are enemies.
Scripture presents a more complete picture.
Jesus said, "They that are whole need not a physician, but they that are sick" (Luke 5:31, KJV), using the ordinary role of physicians as an illustration.
Paul referred to Luke as "the beloved physician" (Colossians 4:14).
And Paul advised Timothy to use a little wine for his stomach and frequent ailments (1 Timothy 5:23), demonstrating that practical remedies were not inherently opposed to faith.
The problem with Asa was not simply that he consulted doctors.
The problem was that, in the chronicler's account, he sought them instead of seeking the Lord.
He repeated the same pattern that had appeared in his political decisions.
When threatened, he depended on Syria rather than God.
When afflicted, he turned to physicians without seeking God.
The repeated spiritual failure was misplaced ultimate dependence.
There is nothing unspiritual about receiving appropriate medical care.
Pray, and seek qualified medical help.
Take prescribed treatment responsibly.
Ask God for wisdom, strength, and healing.
Trust Him whether recovery comes quickly, slowly, or not in the way you hoped.
Faith does not require neglecting the means of care available to us.
But neither should those means replace our relationship with the One who holds our lives.
A hospital can treat a body.
Medicine can address disease.
A skilled physician can provide life-saving care.
But no physician can take the place of God as the ultimate source of our hope.
And now we come to the question that makes Asa's story so haunting.
Why did he refuse to seek the Lord?
Scripture does not reveal his private thoughts.
We cannot know whether he was driven by pride, bitterness, spiritual exhaustion, fear, or some combination of motives.
But the surrounding narrative shows a man who had resisted God's correction and failed to return to the dependence that marked his earlier years.
That is the tragedy.
Not that he became sick.
Not that he needed physicians.
Not even that his physical strength was failing.
The tragedy is that Scripture records his severe suffering without recording a return to the God he had once trusted so completely.
And then comes the final sentence.
"And Asa slept with his fathers, and died in the one and fortieth year of his reign." — 2 Chronicles 16:13 (KJV)
That is how the chapter records the end of his life.
Forty-one years on the throne.
A remarkable beginning.
Important religious reforms.
A miraculous military deliverance.
A public testimony of God's power.
And a final chapter marked by stubbornness and misplaced dependence.
Yet we should not distort his entire legacy.
First Kings 15:14 says that Asa's heart was devoted to the Lord throughout his days, while Chronicles also faithfully records his later failures.
The Bible gives us both truths.
A life can contain genuine faithfulness and serious spiritual failure.
A believer can have a meaningful history with God and still need urgent repentance today.
We must also resist pretending that Asa's final illness gives us complete knowledge of his eternal destiny.
Scripture does not authorize us to pronounce that verdict.
The warning is serious enough without adding what God has not revealed.
And perhaps that makes this story even more piercing.
Because the question is not whether Asa's name appeared in the history books.
It did.
The question is what his final decisions reveal about the danger of allowing yesterday's faithfulness to replace today's surrender.
There are people reading this who once prayed with tears streaming down their faces.
You remember when worship was not a performance.
When opening the Bible felt like coming home.
When you could barely finish a prayer because you were overwhelmed by God's mercy.
When you had nothing to offer Him except a broken heart, and somehow that was enough to bring you to your knees.
You remember the night you begged Jesus to forgive you.
The season when He carried you through grief.
The moment you realized that your sins were greater than you could repair, but His grace was greater still.
And now?
You are not necessarily denying Christ.
You are simply tired.
Distracted.
Guarded.
Maybe disappointed.
You still believe, but you no longer seek Him as you once did.
You have learned how to survive without praying much.
How to make decisions without asking for wisdom.
How to hide your pain behind spiritual language.
How to keep functioning while your soul grows quiet.
And sometimes you wonder why you feel so far from God.
Listen carefully.
The answer is not always that you have committed some dramatic scandal.
Sometimes the distance grows through ordinary self-reliance.
Through the slow habit of carrying burdens God has invited you to bring to Him.
Through becoming so accustomed to handling everything that you forget what it means to surrender anything.
And yet, the Gospel gives us a hope that Asa's tragic final chapter makes us long to hear.
There is another King.
A King greater than Asa.
A King who did not abandon His Father's will when suffering became unbearable.
A King who entered a garden called Gethsemane and faced anguish beyond anything we can fully comprehend.
Jesus Christ.
On the night before His crucifixion, He prayed:
"Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done." — Luke 22:42 (KJV)
Where human kings failed, the Son of God remained obedient.
Where sinful humanity has repeatedly chosen self-reliance, Jesus entrusted Himself to the Father's will.
Where we have resisted correction, defended our pride, and pursued our own way, Christ humbled Himself even unto death on the cross (Philippians 2:8).
And here is the breathtaking difference.
Asa's story shows us the tragedy of a heart that would not seek the Lord in suffering.
Jesus' story shows us the Savior who entered suffering in perfect obedience so that sinners could be reconciled to God.
The feet of King Asa became severely diseased.
The feet of Jesus were pierced in the crucifixion.
But we must not confuse the two.
The Bible does not present Asa's disease as a prophetic symbol of Christ's wounds.
Their connection is not an invented prophecy.
It is a Gospel contrast.
The failing king reminds us of humanity's need.
The crucified and risen King reveals God's provision.
Isaiah 53:5 declares:
"But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed." (KJV)
This is not a promise that every faithful Christian will be physically cured in this present life.
Isaiah's prophecy, understood in the light of Christ's saving work, centers on the suffering Servant bearing sin and bringing restoration to His people.
First Peter 2:24 connects this healing with dying to sin and living unto righteousness.
The deepest human disease is not located in our feet.
It is the sin that separates us from a holy God.
And the greatest healing Christ provides is reconciliation with the Father through His death and resurrection.
That is why the Gospel is not merely an invitation to become a better person.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
He did what we could never do for ourselves.
He bore the judgment our sins deserved.
He offers forgiveness to those who repent and believe in Him.
He does not simply improve our reputation.
He makes reconciliation with God possible.
He does not merely teach us how to conceal our scandals.
He calls us out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
And this is where our Gospel Warrior declaration becomes more than a memorable phrase.
Not because Jesus pretends our sins never happened.
Not because repentance is optional.
Not because consequences always disappear.
But because His mercy can reach the guilty, His forgiveness can cleanse the repentant, and His transforming grace can give a new direction to lives that once seemed hopeless.
Maybe your scandal is public.
People know what you did.
Your family remembers.
Your reputation has suffered.
Maybe your scandal is hidden.
The bitterness you feed.
The pornography you keep returning to.
The pride you refuse to confess.
The resentment you have carried for years.
The spiritual indifference nobody notices because you still look like a committed Christian.
Or maybe your deepest struggle is not a scandal anyone else can see.
Maybe it is the private exhaustion of someone who has been trying to remain strong for everyone else.
You are the one people call when they need prayer.
The one who encourages others.
The one who shares Scripture.
The one who says, "God is faithful," while silently wondering why your own heart feels so empty.
You have become so practiced at being the strong believer that you are afraid to admit you need help.
But Jesus never called you to pretend you were self-sufficient.
He said:
"Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." — Matthew 11:28 (KJV)
Come unto Me.
Not come when you have repaired everything.
Not come when your emotions are under control.
Not come when you can explain why you have drifted.
Come.
With the confusion.
With the shame.
With the stubbornness.
With the questions.
With the tears you have been holding back.
Come to Christ in repentance and faith.
The Savior who receives sinners is not surprised by your weakness.
And His invitation is not permission to continue in rebellion.
His grace calls us to turn from sin and follow Him.
Perhaps you have spent years asking God to remove the pain while resisting what His Word has been exposing in your heart.
Perhaps you have been asking for peace without surrendering the bitterness.
Asking for restoration without admitting the wrong.
Asking for spiritual strength while neglecting the very Word that nourishes faith.
If so, do not use Asa's story to condemn yourself beyond hope.
Use it as a warning that leads you back to Jesus.
Because conviction is not the same as condemnation.
Romans 8:1 declares that there is no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus.
And 1 John 1:9 assures us that God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse those who confess their sins.
Do not turn these promises into an excuse for sin.
Receive them as an invitation to stop hiding.
And if you are suffering from illness right now, please hear this clearly.
Your disease is not proof that God is punishing you.
Your pain does not automatically mean your faith is weak.
Your need for medicine does not mean you have failed spiritually.
Jesus rejected the assumption that a man's blindness must have been caused by his own sin or his parents' sin (John 9:1–3).
Paul lived with an affliction he asked the Lord to remove, and God's answer emphasized the sufficiency of divine grace (2 Corinthians 12:7–10).
Faithful believers can become seriously ill.
Some recover.
Some continue living with chronic conditions.
Some die while trusting Christ.
Our hope is not that believers will never suffer.
Our hope is that Jesus Christ has conquered sin and death, and that those who belong to Him will share in the resurrection life He has promised.
So seek appropriate treatment.
Receive help.
Let others pray with you.
And do not measure God's love by whether your body is healed on the timetable you desire.
The cross has already revealed the depth of His love.
The empty tomb has already declared the victory of His Son.
And His promise of eternal life is greater than the temporary strength of our mortal bodies.
There is another truth here that we desperately need to recover.
Not every successful decision is a spiritually faithful decision.
Asa's alliance with Syria produced immediate results.
But God rebuked the reliance behind it.
That should make us examine the way we measure success.
A business can grow while its owner becomes spiritually cold.
A ministry can attract attention while its leaders neglect prayer and accountability.
A person can gain influence while losing humility.
A family can appear respectable while unforgiveness quietly destroys relationships behind closed doors.
Visible results cannot replace obedience.
Public approval cannot replace faithfulness.
And religious activity cannot substitute for a heart surrendered to Christ.
This is why Gospel-centered discipleship matters so deeply.
We do not merely need another inspirational quote to carry us through the morning.
We need the whole counsel of God's Word.
We need truth that comforts us when we are wounded and confronts us when we are wandering.
We need believers who will pray with us, encourage us, and lovingly call us to repentance when we begin trusting ourselves more than God.
We need to keep returning to Scripture, not to earn salvation, but because the Savior who saves us also calls us to grow in His grace and knowledge.
And that is the heart behind Gospel Warrior.
Not to build a platform around human personalities.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to turn the Gospel into a product.

But to use the opportunities available to us to proclaim Jesus Christ, encourage believers, reach people who are searching for truth, and provide resources that help Christians become more deeply rooted in Scripture.
These resources are intended to help people study God's Word, strengthen their understanding of biblical truth, and grow in their walk with Jesus Christ.
And here is something important.
You do not need to pay for God's love.
You cannot purchase forgiveness, salvation, or the favor of Jesus Christ.
Those gifts are received by grace through faith, not bought with money.
Not out of guilt.
But because freely chosen generosity can be one meaningful way of supporting the spread of biblical teaching and discipleship resources.
The Bible teaches:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
That is the spirit in which we make this invitation.
It is not a required biblical tithe, and it should not replace the responsibilities of generosity, stewardship, and support you have toward your local church and those in genuine need.
But for those who desire to partner with this work, it is a practical opportunity to participate in making more Scripture-centered resources available.
These items are not the Gospel itself.
But because someone connected to you may be carrying a spiritual burden you know nothing about.
A former church member who has quietly drifted away.
A father struggling to lead his family.
A mother praying through exhaustion.
A young believer afraid to admit they are losing their way.
A person who has convinced themselves that Jesus would never receive someone with their history.
You may never know who reads it.
But you can share the truth faithfully and trust God with the results.
There may come a season when the Lord's faithfulness feels distant and you need to remember the difference between trusting God and merely remembering that you once trusted Him.
When was the last time you truly sought the Lord?
Not simply asked Him to bless a decision you had already made.
Not merely repeated a familiar prayer.
Not opened your Bible just to find a verse to post.
When was the last time you came before God with no excuses, no performance, and no attempt to hide what was happening inside you?
When was the last time you said:
"Lord, search me."
"Correct me."
"Forgive me."
"Teach me to trust You again."
Maybe this article has exposed a place where you have become too dependent on your own strength.
Maybe you have been resisting a truth you know you need to face.
Maybe you have been physically suffering and have misunderstood your pain as evidence that God has abandoned you.
Maybe you are simply tired of pretending your spiritual life is healthier than it really is.
Whatever the case, you do not have to turn the comments into a public confession of private details.
You can also share a testimony of a time God taught you to depend on Him, if you feel comfortable doing so.
Someone reading your words may discover that they are not the only person learning how to surrender.
Because the Christian life is not sustained by pretending we never struggle.
It is sustained by the grace of God, through faith in Jesus Christ, as the Holy Spirit works in us to produce repentance, obedience, perseverance, and love.
And now, as we return to Asa's story one final time, notice something.
The Bible tells us that his feet became diseased.
But it does not tell us that his physical condition was his greatest problem.
His greatest documented failure was that he did not seek the Lord.
And that is the question his life leaves behind.
Not merely, "What happened to Asa's feet?"
But, "What happens to us when we stop seeking the God who once delivered us?"
Do not wait until your circumstances become unbearable before returning to prayer.
Do not wait until pride has hardened into bitterness.
Do not wait until years of spiritual neglect have made surrender feel unfamiliar.
And do not confuse God's patience with permission to keep drifting.
Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your heart (Hebrews 3:15).
Turn to Jesus.
If you have never trusted Him as Savior, repent and believe the Gospel.
If you belong to Him but have wandered, confess your sin and return to walking in obedience.
If you are suffering, seek Him honestly and receive the help you need.
If you are strong today, remain humble enough to remember that every breath is a gift.
And if you are standing in the aftermath of decisions you deeply regret, remember that the grace of Christ is greater than the disgrace of a repentant sinner's past.
The King of kings did not come to save people who could prove they had never fallen.
He came to save sinners.
And the One who died on the cross and rose from the grave is worthy of more than the memory of our former devotion.
He is worthy of our trust today.
So here is my final prayer for you.
May God keep your heart tender when correction comes.
May He give you wisdom when decisions become difficult.
May He surround you with people who love you enough to tell you the truth.
May He strengthen you in suffering without allowing suffering to define your identity.
May He guard you from the quiet pride that forgets yesterday's deliverance.
And may He continually draw your eyes back to Jesus Christ, the author and finisher of our faith.
Because one day, every earthly achievement will fade.
Every title will lose its importance.
Every possession will pass into other hands.
Even the strongest body will eventually fail.
But the promise of eternal life in Jesus Christ will remain.
And when that day comes, the greatest treasure will not be the reputation we built, the victories we won, or the strength we once possessed.
It will be the Savior who loved us, redeemed us, and brought us home.
The saddest thing about Asa was not that his feet could no longer carry him—it was that, in his suffering, he would not turn to the God who had carried him before.
